pageCache.pageTitle: Citizenship and British Values - Harris Academy Wimbledon
pageCache.text:
Citizenship and British Values
The Department for Education sets out five clear strands in their definition of British Values, and here at HAWI we all whole heartedly agree with these.
These values are taught in a variety of ways both through our everyday curriculum but also through our Human and Life Skills, SMSC Curriculum and through our Enrichment and Extra-Curricular opportunities. Every member of staff at HAWI is responsible for identifying and delivering key messages linked to the British Values through their everyday interactions with students and by acting as role models by embodying these values in all that they do.
Student voice is incredibly important at HAWI and our Student Council meets regularly to share the voice of all students at HAWI through a democratic approach mirroring that of a national election.
Each member of the Student Council must run for election by creating manifestos and making speeches to gain the support of their House Group who subsequently elect them to become House Leaders and represent their House Group at Student Council. The whole, academy vote for the Students Leadership representatives of Head Boy and Head Girl annually at our HAWI Student Election and the students elected then serve for a one-year term.
The Student Council take feedback from their peers and listen to their thoughts in order to represent them to the best of their ability. This enables all students to have a voice in making change.
The importance of laws, whether they be those that govern the class, the school, or the country, is consistently reinforced at HAWI, and consequently our students possess a strong sense of equality and understanding of what is right and wrong.
We have a rigorous Behaviour and Rewards Policy that is understood by all staff and students and is consistently used both in lessons and outside of the classroom. Students are taught the ‘rules’ of the school along with the value and reasons behind rules and laws, that they govern and protect us, the responsibilities that this involves and the consequences when rules and the law are broken. Students are made aware of how their actions affect others in the community and where needed we work with students to ensure they are better able to make the right choices.
In lessons, students are encouraged to join in and feel free to express their opinion. They are also taught that they will have their opinion challenged and they have a right to reply to this too. This is part of the whole-school Oracy strategy of ABC (Agree, Build & Challenge). Students are encouraged to make good choices and understand that it is their right to receive an empowering education in a safe environment. They are encouraged to exercise their rights and personal freedom, whilst appreciating that everyone is unique and should have their own individual voice. We consistently remind students about creating a ‘Culture of Kindness’ and stereotypes are regularly challenged. This enables our students to feel self-confident and comfortable to express themselves as individuals.
Mutual respect is at the heart of our values. Staff and students treat each other with the utmost respect and courtesy. Students learn that their behaviours affect their rights and those of others. All members of the school community are required to treat each other with respect. This message is communicated to students through assemblies and the Human and Life Skills Curriculum, as well as in everyday interactions with staff and students, and creates a Culture of Kindness where everyone is able to thrive.
Prevention of bullying is very important within the school and is addressed through the Human and Life Skills Curriculum, assemblies, surveys and our Prevention of Bullying Policy. We celebrate Anti-Bullying week with a series of House activities and whole school events to promote difference and equality in our school. Students are also taught about respect and bullying in the online world ensuring that bullying is rare at HAWI.
HAWI is rich in cultural diversity and we are proud to promote and celebrate our different backgrounds and beliefs. Students learn that all members of the school community deserve to be treated with respect and that differences are to be accepted and celebrated.
Throughout our curriculum teachers take opportunities to promote mutual respect and understanding. In Religious Studies this is a particular focus as students learn about all World Religions and are taught about the importance of respecting and understanding different beliefs people have.
Assemblies and the Human and Life Skills Curriculum actively challenge stereotypes and reinforce messages of tolerance and respect for others no matter their ethnicity, beliefs, gender or disability again creating a Culture of Kindness where all students thrive and succeed as a result.

pageCache.text:
Our Vision & Values
Make a Difference
Three words are crucial to how we guide students to be able to ‘make a difference’: independence, integrity and resilience.
Independence means we support students to develop their skills and attributes so they do not have to depend on others and can think and act for themselves. We set challenging targets and raise aspirations so students can achieve success.
Integrity means staff and students must be fair and truthful and have the courage to take the right action in every situation, even when no-one is looking.
Resilience means we give students the tools to recover from difficulties. We show students how taking risks and making mistakes is all part of the learning journey. We also show students how hard work brings success, and support them to persevere with all challenges.
Our Vision & Values

Our Vision & Values

Welcome
Thank you for taking the time to learn more about Harris Academy Wimbledon.
Two years after opening, we moved into our brand-new building which is modern, bright and equipped with state-of-the-art facilities in every area of the curriculum. We are oversubscribed and fortunate to have an amazing level of support from the community with waiting lists for entry into every year group of our academy.
Our academy is an exceptional place to learn, providing an ambitious but happy and inclusive environment. As well as strong pastoral support, we offer an enriching extra-curricular programme with over 40 different activities that students can choose from each week.
As part of the Harris Federation, a highly successful group of academies in and around London, our students also benefit from wider opportunities and resources - ranging from support from the Federation’s highly-regarded team of specialist subject consultants to participation in initiatives such as Harris Experience which aims to prepare the most academically promising students for entry to the top universities in the UK.
We have high expectations of our students of all starting points and abilities. To this end, we offer a tailored learning experience so they can achieve their full potential, with students streamed according to ability. Students who need the most stretch and challenge are grouped together and follow a challenging academic curriculum, but we are ambitious for every kind of learner with provision that includes tutoring and small-group sessions for students who need extra support. All of our classes are in a mixed setting which encourages our girls and boys to work collaboratively and develop mutual respect.
We know that our students will leave us academically successful, but we also want them to be well-rounded individuals with a highly developed social conscience, ready to lead in their communities and beyond. Our motto is ‘make a difference’ and our students and staff give nothing except their very best in pursuit of making a difference to their lives and the lives of others around them.
Three words are crucial to how we guide students to be able to ‘make a difference’: independence, integrity and resilience.
Independence means we support students to develop their skills and attributes so they have everything they need to succeed. We set challenging targets and raise aspirations so every single one of our students reaches their potential.
Integrity means staff and students must be fair and truthful and have the courage to take the right action in every situation, even when no-one is looking.
Resilience means we give students the tools to recover from difficulties. We show students how taking risks and making mistakes is all part of the learning journey. We also show students how hard work brings success, and support them to persevere with all challenges.
Whether you are looking for a Year 7 place, a Sixth Form place or an occasional place somewhere in the middle, please do visit us on our open days and chat to our students and teachers about their experiences here. It really is a wonderful school and we would be delighted to welcome you.
Joanne Larizadeh, Principal

Welcome to HAWI6
HAWI6 is an ambitious, supportive, and high-performing Sixth Form where students achieve exceptional outcomes and take confident steps into their futures.
HAWI6 success reflects the strength of our broad and rigorous curriculum, our personalised guidance, and our commitment to helping every young person shape a pathway that is right for them. Our partnership with King’s College School, Wimbledon, ranked among the top-performing schools in the country, further enriches our provision, offering students access to outstanding academic enrichment, expert teaching collaboration, and inspirational opportunities that raise aspirations even higher.
The impact of this culture of excellence can be seen in the remarkable destinations secured by our students. Many have become the first in our academy’s history to progress to university, including top Russell Group institutions. This year’s offers include University of Cambridge (Geography), King’s College London (Biomedical Science), Durham (Politics and International Relations), York (Accounting and Finance), Exeter (Arabic and Politics), Sheffield (Aerospace Engineering), and many more, spanning competitive fields from Computer Science and Law to Fashion Marketing and Speech and Language Therapy. These achievements speak not only to academic strength, but to the ambition, purpose, and individuality of our learners. At HAWI6, students are supported to thrive, whether their next step is university, apprenticeships, or the world of work, and to leave us equipped, confident, and ready to make their mark.
Discover endless opportunities - expert teaching, tailored support, vibrant community, and the perfect springboard for future success.

Computer Science
What is Computer Science?
Computer science is the study of computers and computing, including their theoretical and algorithmic foundations, hardware and software, and their uses for processing information. The discipline of Computer Science includes the study of algorithms and data structures, computer, and network design, modelling data and information processes, and artificial intelligence. Computer Science draws some of its foundations from mathematics and engineering and therefore incorporates a range of transferable techniques.
Why do we teach Computer Science at HAWI?
Technology is at the forefront of developments in all areas of society. Computer Science is a course that challenges students to solve real world problems developing their problem solving, logical thinking skills that helps to prepare students in a volatile, uncertain, and ever-changing world. In addition to this, educating students in Computer Science will equip them and empower them to be successful individuals in a digital age. Students must be competent in using computers whether it be to create a file, write a report, or researching a certain subject. At HAWI we strive to ensure all students leave us as digitally literate and competent users of all aspects of IT.
How do we teach Computer Science at HAWI?
The curriculum is split into units which:
Interleaved throughout the curriculum are computational thinking and problem-solving skills that are taught using ‘Big Questions’ with the intent on students being able to confidently answer these.
Across all key stages we aim to build on previous units and challenge students to use their theoretical and programming skills to solve the problems put to them. Students will also go through what is known as the ‘system life cycle’ where they will have opportunities to analyse, design, develop, test, and evaluate their solutions in which they have used their problem solving and logical thinking skills. How do we make Computer Science memorable at HAWI?
Computer Science lessons aim to bring learning to life, however, alongside this the curriculum at HAWI has many memorable moments. These include visits to Bletchley Park where students will take part in a Computer Science ciphers workshop, and completion of the IDEA award. The Inspiring Digital Enterprise Award, known as iDEA is an international award-winning programme that helps students develop digital, enterprise and employability skills for free. Through a series of online challenges, students can win career-enhancing badges, unlock new opportunities, and gain industry-recognised Awards that help them stand out from the crowd. There is also optional enrichment in Computer Science in which students will use pocket sized computers called microbits, to further improve their programming skills on a piece of hardware they do not see in normal lessons.

Drama
What is Drama?
Drama is the study of texts, plays and exploring the world of theatre; students are able to take on different characters learning how to become them through using vocal and physical skills. Drama is also a tool for exploring other subjects as well as helping students understand the world around them. Drama often links to the English Curriculum, with similar texts taught in both subjects at HAWI, such as Romeo and Juliet. Then through Drama students are given the opportunity to develop their spoken language, reading, which in turn helps them with their writing skills.
Why do we teach Drama at HAWI?
Drama is an essential subject to help students build self-confidence, develop teamwork, communication and leadership skills, all whilst exploring and challenging perceptions about the world they live in and themselves. Through powerful knowledge, a student can explore a new role, try out and problem solve very real problems from their own life or problems faced by characters in literature. For example, exploring the character of Christopher in ‘The Curious Incident of a Dog in the Night-time’, allows students to experience and develop their understanding of someone who sees the world very differently. Drama plays a vital role in developing oracy by giving students regular opportunities to speak, listen and respond in meaningful contexts. Through activities such as role play, improvisation and group discussion, pupils learn to articulate their ideas clearly, adapt their language for different audiences and build confidence in expressing themselves. Drama also strengthens active listening skills, as students must interpret and respond to the words, emotions and intentions of others. By encouraging collaboration, creativity and verbal communication, drama provides a powerful foundation for effective speaking and listening across the curriculum and beyond.
How do we teach Drama at HAWI?
The drama curriculum is a practical artistic subject and ranges from student's structured exploration through to classroom improvisation, polished presentation to performances of classic play texts through the work of Shakespeare for example in Year 7 students study Romeo and Juliet and in Year 8 Students study Macbeth. Through the practical exploration of Drama, students will begin to develop a range of theatrical skills focussing on the use of voice and physicality to bring about the successful creation of character. Whilst developing such skills, students will also be introduced to the workings of the theatre and the function of light, sound, props, and staging in bringing about an effective performance which is covered throughout KS3 and 4. This will allow students to develop their powers of expression, communication and aesthetic understanding. There are four main areas students gain knowledge in through the drama curriculum:
Creating and Developing
Applying Theatrical Skills
Demonstrating Knowledge and Understanding
Evaluation and Analysis
Across the key stages our curriculum is taught using ‘Big Questions’ which students look to answer through each unit of work as their powerful drama knowledge develops. We look to use high challenge in every lesson to push our students, for example by looking at key drama practitioners such as Artaud and Brecht, students can work in different styles and explore different genres.
How do we make Drama memorable at HAWI?
Alongside drama lessons, the curriculum at HAWI is comprised of many memorable moments which bring the subject to life. These include our extensive extra-curricular programme where students are given many opportunities to perform, for example the Whole School Production, as well as being part of the Lower and Upper School Drama Club, where they will work on putting on the production of a play. We have our annual Summer Arts Festival where we run several performing arts workshops and put on several performances, music, dance, and drama come together for a week of celebration. There are also LAMDA enrichments that we offer which gives students a chance to earn their grade 1 or 2 in devised theatre. Alongside this we have outside practitioners who are working in the world of theatre who come and meet our students, for examples actors, directors, producers, and lighting designers who can inspire our students to think about the different roles in the arts. We also look to take students to the theatre several times a year, increasing their cultural capital.

Music
"Music is all around us. It is the soundtrack to our lives. Music connects us through people and places in our ever-changing world. It is creative, collaborative, celebratory and challenging. In our schools, music can bring communities together through the shared endeavour of whole-school singing, ensemble playing, experimenting with the creative process and, through the love of listening to friends and fellow pupils, performing. The sheer joy of music making can feed the soul of a school community, enriching each student while strengthening the shared bonds of support and trust which make a great school... Music has a rare and unique ability to bring people together; music making can make a whole class, school and community feel connected to others and part of something bigger."
– DfE Model Music Curriculum (2021)
At HAWI, we believe music is far more than a subject—it is a powerful form of expression, a means of connection, and a source of joy. Music inspires creativity, builds confidence, develops resilience, and opens doors to cultures, traditions and experiences from across the world. Whether performing, composing, listening or creating, music enables students to find their voice and become part of something bigger than themselves.
Why do we teach Music at HAWI?
At HAWI, we believe every child deserves a rich and inspiring music education. Music is a universal language that transcends barriers, communicates emotion, and brings people together. Through music, students develop creativity, discipline, perseverance and self-confidence, while gaining a deeper understanding of the world around them.
Our curriculum is carefully designed around the powerful musical knowledge and experiences that all students are entitled to. We celebrate the music that matters to our students while broadening their horizons through exposure to a diverse range of genres, styles, cultures and traditions. We aim to ignite curiosity, nurture creativity and foster a lifelong appreciation of music.
By engaging with music as performers, composers and critical listeners, students develop not only musical skills but also the confidence to express themselves, collaborate with others and embrace new challenges. We want every student to leave HAWI with a lasting love of music and the belief that music can enrich their lives long beyond the classroom.
Music at HAWI also supports students in exploring future pathways within the creative industries. Through curriculum learning, enrichment opportunities and performance experiences, students gain valuable transferable skills including teamwork, communication, creativity, resilience and leadership. Students are introduced to the wide range of careers available within the music industry and the wider creative sector, including performance, composition, music production, sound engineering, arts management, teaching and music therapy. These experiences help students to develop confidence in their abilities and understand how their musical skills can support future study, employment and lifelong participation in the arts.
HAWI as a Lead School for Music
Harris Academy Wimbledon is proud to be recognised as one of Merton's Lead Schools for Music, playing a key role in supporting high-quality music education across the borough. As a Lead School, we work collaboratively with local schools, music organisations and cultural partners to champion inclusive musical opportunities, share expertise and ensure that every young person has access to a rich and meaningful music education.
Our unique position is enhanced by our close partnership with Merton Music Foundation (MMF), the lead organisation of the Merton Music Education Hub. Located immediately next door to the academy, MMF provides exceptional opportunities for our students through instrumental tuition, ensembles, choirs, orchestras, music technology programmes and large-scale performances. This partnership enables students to access specialist teaching, high-quality progression routes and a wealth of musical experiences that extend beyond the classroom.
Together, Harris Academy Wimbledon and Merton Music Foundation share a commitment to nurturing musical talent, widening participation and ensuring that music remains a vibrant and transformative part of young people's lives. Through our role as a Lead School, we contribute to a thriving culture of music-making across the local community while providing our students with outstanding opportunities to develop as performers, composers and creative musicians.
How do we teach Music at HAWI?
Our music curriculum is built around a carefully sequenced spiral model, enabling students to revisit and deepen their understanding of the three core disciplines of music: performing, composing and listening. As students progress through the key stages, they encounter increasingly sophisticated musical concepts, skills and repertoire, building confidence and expertise over time.
Learning is organised through engaging units of study that explore music from a wide range of historical periods, genres, cultures and traditions. Each unit is driven by a thought-provoking Big Question, encouraging students to think critically, make connections and develop their musical understanding as they seek answers through practical and theoretical learning.
Music theory is woven into every lesson, ensuring students develop fluency in musical language and notation. This knowledge empowers them to access and engage with music independently, opening pathways to lifelong music-making. Alongside this, creativity sits at the heart of our curriculum. Students are encouraged to experiment, take risks and express themselves through singing, instrumental performance, composition and music technology, developing both technical skill and artistic confidence.
How do we make Music memorable at HAWI?
Music is at the heart of school life at HAWI, creating unforgettable experiences that inspire students and build a sense of belonging. Beyond the classroom, students have access to a vibrant programme of musical opportunities that allow them to develop their talents, discover new passions and create lasting memories.
Our team of visiting specialist instrumental teachers provides weekly one-to-one tuition in drums, guitar, piano, singing, strings, woodwind and brass, enabling students to flourish as musicians. A wide range of extra-curricular ensembles welcomes students of all abilities and backgrounds, ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to participate, perform and succeed. Whether joining a choir, performing in a string ensemble, playing in a band or attending the popular Friday morning Music Theory Club, every student has the opportunity to develop their musical talents and find their place within HAWI's thriving musical community.
Students can also take part in enrichment activities that develop skills in music technology or provide the opportunity to learn a brass instrument from scratch. These experiences often become the starting point for a lifelong musical journey.
One of the most exciting opportunities available to students is HAWI Rocks, our unique Saturday music programme that brings together young musicians to form and perform in real pop and rock bands. Open to students from across the local community, HAWI Rocks provides specialist tuition in drums, guitar, keyboards and vocals, while developing ensemble skills, confidence and stagecraft. Students rehearse and perform a carefully selected repertoire of contemporary pop and rock music, working collaboratively with expert tutors and fellow musicians. Through regular rehearsals and performances, HAWI Rocks nurtures creativity, teamwork and a love of live music, providing students with an authentic band experience that is both challenging and rewarding.
Performance is a cornerstone of musical life at HAWI. Throughout the year, students showcase their achievements through a variety of exciting events, including the Winter Celebration, where every Year 7 student joins together in a mass choir, the spectacular annual musical theatre production, which brings together students from across the school in a collaborative celebration of the performing arts, and the Summer Arts Festival, a week-long celebration of creativity culminating in performances from ensembles and soloists.
Through these opportunities, students experience the thrill of performance, the power of collaboration and the joy of creating music together. At HAWI, we strive to ensure that every student leaves with treasured musical memories, newfound confidence and a lifelong appreciation of the transformative power of music.

English
English is the study of language and literature, explored through novels, plays, poetry, and non-fiction texts. Students analyse, debate, and critically evaluate both classic and contemporary works, considering how writers shape meaning and influence readers. Alongside this, they develop their own voice, engaging in discussion and purposeful talk, and crafting their own fiction and non-fiction writing with increasing confidence and control.
Why do we teach English at HAWI?
Engaging with literature and a wide range of written and spoken texts enables students to explore worlds beyond their own experience and to deepen their understanding of what it means to be human. At HAWI, we aim to nurture a lifelong love of reading through a curriculum that balances rich literary heritage texts with modern and thought-provoking voices. Across Key Stages 3–5, students encounter challenging texts and ideas which invite them to grapple with themes such as power, identity, conflict, morality and social responsibility.
Through carefully sequenced units, students develop their understanding of how writers reflect and shape the political, social and cultural contexts in which they write. While our curriculum draws strongly on influential and canonical works, we also create deliberate opportunities—through poetry, protest literature and thematic study—for students to encounter a broader range of perspectives and experiences. This equips students with powerful knowledge that enables them to think critically, engage with differing viewpoints and develop empathy.
By deepening students’ knowledge of literature, language and the wider world, we empower them to question the society they are part of and to express their own ideas with increasing confidence, precision and sophistication.
How do we teach English at HAWI?
Across the key stages, our curriculum is shaped by ‘Big Questions’ which guide students’ thinking as their knowledge of literature and language develops. At Key Stage 3, these questions are unified by an overarching theme for each year, enabling students to make meaningful connections between the texts and ideas they encounter. The themes—Year 7: Exploring Different Voices; Year 8: Conflict and Change; and Year 9: Power—allow students to situate their learning within broader conceptual frameworks, while also preparing them for the disciplinary demands and conceptual complexity of Key Stage 4.
Our curriculum is underpinned by four threshold concepts: Layers of Language, Authorial Intent, Structure, and Punctuation, Grammar and Vocabulary. These concepts are revisited and deepened over time, enabling students to build secure, transferable knowledge as they move from foundational understanding in Key Stage 3 to increasingly sophisticated analysis at Key Stage 4 and beyond.
In the classroom, we place a strong emphasis on high-quality talk, with structured discussion embedded into every lesson. Students are routinely supported to rehearse, refine and extend their ideas verbally before crafting them into precise, analytical writing. Through this deliberate integration of reading, writing and spoken language, students develop the confidence and control needed to communicate their ideas clearly, thoughtfully and effectively.
How do we make English memorable at HAWI?
Alongside classroom study, our English curriculum is enriched by a range of carefully planned experiences which bring texts and ideas to life. These include visits to the theatre to see performances such as Othello at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon, The Crucible, The Hunger Games, and Romeo and Juliet at The Globe Theatre. Experiencing these works in performance deepens students’ understanding of character, theme and interpretation, while broadening their engagement with significant literary texts.
Beyond the classroom, Curiosity Days and visiting speaker events enable students to engage with authors, poets and spoken word artists. Author visits, most recently including Tola Okogwu, Christopher Edge and Savita Kalhan, are designed to encourage students to engage more deeply with reading, fostering enjoyment while also offering insight into the writing process and the contemporary relevance of literature. During Curiosity Days, students have also taken part in a literary walking tour of London, connecting literature to place and context.
Students also develop their skills in public speaking and debate through participation in the Jack Petchey “Speak Out” Challenge, as well as MACE, Debate Mate and ESU competitions. These experiences build confidence and enable students to articulate their ideas with clarity and conviction.

History and Politics
History is the study of the past and its relevance to the present enables young people to make sense of the world they live in and explore the role they can play in it. Engaging with the histories of diverse people in the UK and their relationship to the rest of the world is of pivotal importance in the growth and development of an inclusive community.
Why do we teach history at HAWI?
Learning the methods of historical enquiry enables students to navigate the offering of information and approach it with the necessary critical thinking. Through this powerful academic knowledge, history at HAWI enables students to locate themselves and their world within a larger and deeper understanding of time. Students will be able to discern the changes, continuities, similarities and differences in a diverse range of histories and interpretations of the past. This curriculum will provide a path for students to develop historical thinking to understand the past, its resonance in the present and its potential significance for the future.
How do we teach history at HAWI?
The KS3 and KS4 curricula aim to:
All schemes of learning will be delivered through historical enquiries to ensure that the rich curricular knowledge is supported by continuously evolving historical thinking. Enquiries will include thematic and period studies to promote the development of a sense of chronology and the deep understanding of key periods and events. These challenging enquiry questions are underpinned by key second-order concepts, such as similarity and difference, causation, and change and continuity. These concepts are revisited throughout KS3 and become increasingly challenging as the curriculum progresses into Key Stage Four. Each lesson includes learning challenges that students work towards when answering the enquiry question posed in each unit of work.
How do we make history memorable at HAWI?
Alongside history lessons, the curriculum at HAWI is comprised of many memorable moments which bring the history to life for our students. These include visits to historical monuments such as the Tower of London which supports students understanding of Norman Britain, which they will study at the beginning of KS3. Alongside these excursions, there are optional enrichment opportunities in history in which students engage with diverse histories by analysing historical events beyond the classroom curriculum and they apply their powerful historical knowledge to better understand the world we live in today. We also offer History Film Club whereby students critically analyse films based on historical events and make judgements on the validity and accuracy of these interpretations as historical sources. These opportunities enable students to develop their communication and social skills, whilst also inspiring students and instilling a greater interest for the subject.

pageCache.pageTitle: Art & Photography - Subjects - Harris Academy Wimbledon
pageCache.text:
Art & Photography
At HAWI, our vision is to develop imaginative, skilled and confident artists who are curious about the world around them and courageous in expressing their own ideas. We aim for all students to leave with the knowledge, technical skill and creative confidence to think critically, communicate visually and make meaningful contributions through art. We believe creativity has the power to transform lives, and our curriculum nurtures students who are reflective, resilient and willing to challenge conventions in pursuit of original ideas.
Art is a dynamic and expressive subject that enables students to explore ideas, communicate emotions and understand the world through visual language. It combines creativity, observation, technical skill and critical thinking, allowing students to experiment with materials, processes and concepts to create personal and meaningful outcomes.
At HAWI, we believe Art is about far more than producing beautiful work—it is about questioning, exploring and discovering. Students are encouraged to investigate ideas with curiosity, challenge assumptions and develop their own artistic voice. Through experimentation, reflection and refinement, they learn to solve visual problems, embrace creative risk-taking and understand that great art is driven by enquiry as much as technical skill.
We believe every student should have the opportunity to experience the transformative power of creativity. Art develops imagination, resilience and confidence while encouraging students to question, interpret and respond to the world around them.
Our curriculum develops:
Creativity and imagination – generating original ideas and developing personal responses.
Observation and visual literacy – learning to see, analyse and communicate through drawing and making.
Technical skill – mastering a broad range of materials, techniques and artistic processes.
Critical thinking – analysing artists, cultures and ideas while evaluating and refining their own work.
Confidence and independence – developing ownership of creative decisions and personal expression.
Cultural understanding – exploring diverse artists, movements and traditions from across the world.
We also introduce students to the vast range of careers within the creative industries, including fine art, architecture, illustration, graphic design, animation, photography, fashion, product design, curation, museum education and the wider cultural sector, helping students understand the relevance of Art far beyond the classroom.
Our curriculum is built around ambitious, project-based learning where students investigate artists, develop technical skills and create increasingly personal outcomes. Each project combines practical making with critical thinking, encouraging students to experiment, reflect and continually refine their work.
Rather than teaching isolated techniques, we teach students how artists think. Every project develops technical expertise alongside conceptual understanding, enabling students to become increasingly independent, creative and reflective practitioners.
At KS3, students complete a carefully sequenced programme of projects that develop drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, ceramics, mixed media and digital processes.
Projects are designed to progressively build knowledge and confidence, revisiting key artistic concepts whilst introducing increasingly sophisticated techniques and ideas. Observational drawing forms the backbone of the curriculum, underpinning every area of artistic practice.
Students learn through:
Project-based learning inspired by artists, cultures, history and contemporary issues.
Developing observational drawing as the foundation of artistic practice.
Experimenting with a broad range of materials, techniques and processes.
Researching artists and analysing how meaning is communicated through visual language.
Recording ideas through sketchbooks that document experimentation, reflection and refinement.
Creating increasingly independent and personal final outcomes.
Creativity sits at the heart of every project, with students encouraged to experiment, embrace challenge and develop their own artistic identity.
Students build upon their KS3 experiences through increasingly independent projects that demand greater technical proficiency, conceptual understanding and personal creativity.
Students can progress onto:
These pathways allow students to:
Develop sustained personal investigations.
Refine specialist practical skills across a wide range of media.
Produce ambitious portfolios demonstrating creativity, experimentation and technical control.
Strengthen critical analysis, evaluation and independent thinking.
Our highly successful A Level Art course provides students with an ambitious and intellectually challenging experience, consistently achieving exceptional outcomes while preparing students for higher education and careers within the creative industries.
Students are encouraged to think like contemporary artists—questioning assumptions, exploring ideas in depth and developing highly personal bodies of work that demonstrate creativity, technical excellence and critical understanding.
A defining feature of our curriculum is the Strange Forms Project, an intensive programme that challenges students to rethink everything they know about art. Through sustained investigation, students question materials, processes, scale, context and meaning whilst exploring contemporary artistic practice in exceptional depth. They experiment with sculpture, installation, photography, mixed media, performance and conceptual approaches, discovering that art is as much about asking powerful questions as it is about producing successful outcomes.
Rather than simply learning about artists, students become artists—developing independent lines of enquiry, embracing uncertainty, taking creative risks and constructing their own visual language. This philosophy produces confident, intellectually curious young artists capable of creating ambitious, sophisticated and deeply personal work.
Students benefit from opportunities to work with and learn from:
Practising artists and photographers.
Designers, architects and creative professionals.
Higher education providers, galleries and creative industry specialists.
Through workshops, artist talks and demonstrations, students gain valuable insight into professional creative practice and future career pathways.
First-hand experiences are central to our curriculum and play a vital role in inspiring creativity.
Students benefit from visits including:
Year 7: The National Gallery.
Year 8: The National Portrait Gallery and The National Gallery.
GCSE and A Level: Visits to London's leading museums and galleries including Tate Modern, Tate Britain, the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Saatchi Gallery and major temporary exhibitions to support research, idea development and independent investigation.
These experiences enable students to encounter original artworks, deepen their cultural understanding and appreciate the role of art within society.
We provide a rich programme of opportunities beyond the classroom, including:
Arts Week exhibitions celebrating student achievement.
Artist workshops and gallery visits.
Photography club and darkroom experiences.
Competitions and collaborative creative projects.
Opportunities to contribute to school productions, installations, displays and community exhibitions.
These opportunities allow students to extend their learning, develop leadership and celebrate creativity within the wider school community.
We believe Art should inspire curiosity, creativity and confidence that lasts long after students leave school.
Students experience:
The satisfaction of mastering challenging artistic techniques and producing work of exceptional quality.
Opportunities to explore diverse media including drawing, painting, printmaking, ceramics, photography, sculpture and mixed media.
Projects that encourage personal expression whilst engaging with artists, cultures, philosophy and contemporary issues.
A culture that celebrates experimentation, resilience, curiosity and thoughtful creative risk-taking.
Regular opportunities to exhibit work, celebrate success and contribute to the cultural life of the school.
Through these experiences, students leave HAWI as confident, independent and thoughtful young artists who understand both the technical discipline and the transformative power of creativity. They develop the knowledge, resilience and ambition to continue making, questioning and creating throughout their lives, whatever path they choose to follow.

Geography
Geography is the study of physical and human processes and how the relationships between these processes can lead to changes on the surface of the earth. Geography is crucial to understanding the world around us, not just looking at what happens but delving deeper to understand why this happens allowing students to make sense of the world around them.
Why do we teach Geography at HAWI?
Geography equips students with the knowledge to think about the world in new ways; recognising human and physical interactions which shape the planet, appreciating different cultures and ways of life, and understanding contemporary human and environmental challenges. Through this powerful academic knowledge, geography at HAWI enables students to engage in debates both local to them and on a global scale. For example, the impact regeneration will have in High Path, the success and failures of the Ultra Low Emission Zone in London, the influence of geology on climatic hazard risk in the UK, and global disparities in wealth and subsequent issues which arise.
How do we teach Geography at HAWI?
The curriculum is split into units which focus on both systematic and regional geography. Systematic geography focuses on processes and theory, whilst regional considers how these processes influence a place. In the topic Gazing at Glaciers students explore how glacial processes influence the characteristics of the Himalayas, an example of how systematic geography (glacial processes) and regional geography (the Himalayas) are taught in a single unit of study.
Interleaved throughout the curriculum are geographical skills such as map reading, Geographical Information Systems (GIS), and geographical-data analysis and presentation.
Across the key stages our curriculum is taught using ‘Big Questions’ which students look to answer as their powerful geographical knowledge develops through each unit. These challenging enquiry questions are underpinned by five core concepts (which we call our ‘Big Ideas’). These are: Development, Climate, Human and Physical Interactions, Sustainability, and Geomorphology. These Big Ideas are revisited throughout Key Stage 3 and become increasingly complex and challenging as the curriculum progresses into Key Stage Four. Learning challenges within each lesson work towards answering the Big Questions posed in each unit of work.
How do we make Geography memorable at HAWI?
Alongside geography lessons, the curriculum at HAWI is comprised of many memorable moments which bring the subject to life. These include visits to the River Wandle as part of a local fieldwork study, a and GCSE fieldwork exploring air pollution and the coastal landscapes in Kent. Year 8 students also have the opportunity to take part in Mission Save the Planet, an engaging programme that explores sustainable development in the local area through a visit to the regenerated Battersea Power Station. Students also investigate the causes, consequences and solutions to climate change, complemented by educational visits to the London Wetland Centre and ZSL London Zoo. Alongside these excursions, students have the opportunity to meet geography graduates who have made a career from the subject for example in renewable energy, sustainable finance, or international development. There is also optional enrichment in geography in which students engage with current affairs by interrogating news stories, applying their powerful geographical knowledge to better understand the world. Year 9 students also take part in Duke of Edinburgh where they develop their map and navigation skills. In addition, there is an annual cross-Federation Geography Quiz in which students in Year 7 and 8 compete for the honour of being the best geographers in the Federation!

Maths and Economics
What is Mathematics?
Mathematics is a creative and highly interconnected discipline that has been developed over centuries, providing the solution to some of history's most intriguing problems. It is essential to everyday life, critical to science, technology and engineering, and necessary for financial literacy and most forms of employment. A high-quality mathematics education provides a foundation for understanding the world, developing the ability to reason mathematically, appreciate the beauty and power of mathematics, and fosters a sense of enjoyment and curiosity about the subject. Mathematics enables pupils to become confident, resilient problem-solvers who can think logically, make connections and apply their knowledge in a wide range of contexts.
Why do we teach Mathematics at HAWI?
At HAWI, we believe that every pupil deserves an ambitious mathematics education which equips them with the knowledge, skills and confidence to succeed in school and beyond. Mathematics provides pupils with powerful knowledge that helps them understand and interpret the world around them, think logically, solve problems and make informed decisions.
Our curriculum develops fluency, reasoning and problem-solving alongside resilience, curiosity and independence. We want pupils to see mathematics as a connected discipline rather than a collection of isolated methods, enabling them to make links between concepts and apply their knowledge in a range of contexts.
Mathematics opens doors to future study and employment. By ensuring that all pupils develop secure mathematical understanding, we aim to raise aspirations and provide access to a broad range of academic and career pathways. Ultimately, we want every pupil to leave HAWI with a positive relationship with mathematics and the confidence to use it effectively throughout their lives.
How do we teach Mathematics at HAWI?
Our mathematics curriculum is built upon the Harris Federation Scheme of Work and is carefully sequenced so that knowledge and skills build cumulatively over time. Concepts are taught in a coherent order, with new learning regularly linked to prior knowledge, enabling pupils to deepen their understanding and retain key mathematical ideas in the long term. Each topic is framed by a 'Big Question' which highlights the powerful knowledge pupils are expected to learn and remember, with each lesson’s aims broken into a learning challenge and an extra challenge, both of which give students a good understanding of what they are learning.
At Key Stage 3, pupils are taught in ability streams whilst accessing a shared, ambitious curriculum. All pupils study the same core mathematical content, ensuring that prior attainment does not limit access to mathematical knowledge. Teachers use carefully planned modelling, questioning, vocabulary instruction and responsive teaching to provide appropriate support and challenge for all learners.
Reasoning, problem-solving and mathematical communication are central to our curriculum. Through structured discussion, pupils explain their thinking, justify their methods and evaluate the reasoning of others. Teachers deliberately develop pupils' use of precise mathematical language through strategies such as Write, Turn and Talk, helping them to become confident and articulate mathematicians.
At Key Stage 4, pupils follow either the Foundation or Higher pathway, with teaching designed to maximise achievement and prepare pupils for further study. For pupils with a particular aptitude for the subject, opportunities such as GCSE Further Mathematics provide additional challenge and preparation for A Level Mathematics or Further Mathematics, which remains one of the most popular subjects at HAWI.
How do we make Mathematics memorable at HAWI?
We believe that memorable experiences help pupils develop a deeper appreciation of mathematics and its relevance beyond the classroom. Alongside lessons, pupils engage in a wide range of enrichment opportunities designed to inspire curiosity, promote challenge and foster a love of learning.
Pupils regularly participate in mathematics competitions, including monthly quizzes, Federation competitions and the UK Mathematics Trust (UKMT) Challenges. Whole-school events such as Number Day and Pi Day celebrate mathematics through puzzles, investigations and collaborative activities that encourage participation and enjoyment across all year groups.
Educational visits, including trips to Bletchley Park and the London Eye, enable pupils to experience how mathematics underpins developments in cryptography, engineering, architecture and technology. We also work with organisations such as Maths4Girls, helping pupils connect with STEM role models and explore the diverse opportunities that mathematics can unlock.
Selected Year 9 pupils are encouraged to attend Royal Institution Masterclasses, where they explore rich mathematical ideas beyond the classroom curriculum through hands-on workshops led by experts. At Key Stage 5, students are further supported through university outreach programmes and preparation for admissions tests such as TMUA and STEP, helping them access competitive courses and careers in mathematically rich disciplines. Through these experiences, pupils develop ambition, deepen their understanding and recognise the value of mathematics in the wider world.

Latin
Latin was the language spoken by the Ancient Romans which then became the foundation of what we now call ‘Romance Languages’ – Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, French and many more. Latin challenges students to analyse the grammar, syntax and root meaning of words which strengthens their understanding of English. Latin equips students with the tools to read and understand original Latin texts. Through this, students unlock the ancient culture which pathed the way for the modern western world.
Why do we teach Latin at HAWI?
Learning Latin provides an opening to Roman culture and fosters students’ curiosity and understanding of the Classical World. Latin will enable students to understand ideas, thoughts and different aspects of life in the Roman Empire through translation and analysis of Latin texts. Latin is a stepping-stone for learning other modern foreign languages as well as enabling students to gain a deeper understanding of English. It also provides a strong foundation in linguistic and cultural competence, enabling students to break the boundaries of time and space and access knowledge and understanding of the ancient world, through reading and responding to its language and literature.
How do we teach Latin at HAWI?
Our Key Stage 3 curriculum follows the Cambridge Latin Course to introduce our students to Latin vocabulary and grammar centred around specific topics (e.g., Roman daily life, business, theatre and gladiators). This allows our students to delve into the Ancient Roman World, understanding their culture and way of living, whilst beginning to learn the Latin language. Our curriculum follows ‘Big Questions’ that challenge students to think across topics, Latin language and culture – a skill that prepares them for GCSE, A Level and further education in Latin, Classics and many other subjects.
Across Key Stage 3 and 4 our students develop powerful linguistic and analytical knowledge and skills that enable them to translate and analyse Latin texts. The importance of drawing on contextual knowledge during text analysis is a skill that students practice in Key Stage 3 and refine throughout Key Stage 4. As students progress into Key Stage 4 they tackle more complex grammar and syntax, equipping them with the knowledge to translate and analyse original Latin texts from authors such as Horace, Ovid and Virgil. By the end of Key Stage 4, students have a deep understanding of the language and culture of the Classical World.
How do we make Latin memorable at HAWI?
To complement Latin lessons at HAWI, our curriculum includes educational visits, lectures from external speakers and extracurricular opportunities that help bring Latin and the Ancient World to life. For Year 7, alongside learning about the Roman Baths in the Spring term, a trip to the Roman Baths in Bath allows students to see the magnificent building itself and hear from expert Classicists about how the Baths were an integral part of Roman social life. For Year 8, we strive to plan a trip to Pompeii, Italy to visit the town that was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius. In Year 9, focussing more on next steps and opportunities that come with a further education in Latin and Classics, we invite Classicists to HAWI to speak on their experiences with Latin and Classics and enlighten our students on the benefits of studying the Ancient World (e.g., in 2021 we had a lecture from Professor Edith Hall about her career and life as a Classicist). In addition to this, we have a longstanding relationship with King’s College School in which their Year 11 and Sixth Form students come to HAWI on Friday afternoons to run an extracurricular club that complements our curriculum and the needs of our students. Annually, we also attend the Latin Spelling Bee which takes place at Harris Chafford Hundred. This improves our students vocabulary knowledge whilst enabling them to network with peers and avid Classicists.

pageCache.pageTitle: Physical Education - Subjects - Harris Academy Wimbledon
pageCache.text:
Physical Education
The physical education curriculum at Harris Academy Wimbledon will inspire all students to succeed in both competitive and physically demanding activities. The curriculum is designed to stretch and challenge all students to achieve their personal best, both physically and mentally. Through the curriculum, students will develop a true love of physical exercise which will encourage lifelong participation and the potential to improve mental health and wellbeing.
Why do we teach PE at HAWI?
PE and sport at Harris Wimbledon has an integral role in developing well rounded individuals through; lessons, inter/intra competitions, enrichment and external sporting opportunities. Offering a wide range of sporting opportunities is crucial to the development of resilience, confidence, competence and leadership all of which are good characteristics that support a successful and fulfilling life. Pressurised situations provide an opportunity for students to develop skills learnt and apply them in a realistic sporting scenario, which will further develop the student’s ability to perform under pressure which is a great life skill.
How do we teach PE at HAWI?
PE at Harris Academy Wimbledon has a different focus each academic year. Each year builds upon the previous, creating a physically literate person across a range of sports. This will enable students to find ‘their’ sports, that they feel confident in continuing outside of school and to an even higher level of excellence.
Our pedagogical approach in PE is built around appropriate challenge, inclusion and meaningful game-based learning. Students are set and grouped carefully so that lessons can be pitched at the right level, allowing all students to experience success while being stretched physically, technically and tactically. Within these groups, teachers use a games-based approach where skills are taught, refined and applied in realistic sporting contexts. This ensures students understand not only how to perform a skill, but when, why and how to use it effectively within competitive situations. Groupings remain flexible where appropriate, allowing students to develop confidence, leadership, teamwork and tactical understanding across a range of activities.
Year 7- Development of fundamental movement skills and beginning to apply them to small isolated and game related activities.
Year 8- Refining fundamental movement skills and developing and understand how these skills link together to be able to perform in competitive game situations.
Year 9- Further develop the understanding of match play, through teaching strategies, rules, passages of play. Students will critically analyse and plan small teaching sessions to develop their ability to lead, umpire and teach.
Year 10- Within core PE the curriculum will focus on the importance of a healthy active lifestyle. To ensure students understand the importance they will gain the opportunity to choose from an extensive list of sports, to which they can apply previously learnt fundamental movement skills and transfer the skills to participate in new sporting scenarios.
Year 11- Greater focus is placed on the physical, mental and social benefits of sport, alongside the importance of a good nutritious diet. Students will have the opportunity to choose what sport they would like to participate in, on a half termly basis. This will establish an independent element toward sport and exercise, which will set the students in good stead for life-long participation in sport.
How do we make PE memorable at HAWI?
The extensive extracurricular programme provides all students, including those from less advantaged backgrounds, the opportunity to take part in further coaching and sport focussed coaching. This extra provision enables students to access opportunities which could inspire students to participate in a variety of sports and exercise after their time with Harris Academy Wimbledon. The PE curriculum is in place as the stimulus to grow a passion for sport. Students may wish to pursue their passions further through school clubs, which are well linked to local clubs. In addition we host an abundance of sporting house competitions and external fixtures, culminating in our annual sports day which all students take part either as a participant or sport leaders.

Religious Studies
At a surface level, Religious Studies is a study of a variety of religious beliefs and ideas. However, there is much more to be gained from studying Religious Studies than an understanding of the various world religions and their perspectives. Students will explore and engage with challenging questions that underpin the human experience. Religious Studies offers students an opportunity to understand the foundation of our culture and identity, as well as deepening their understanding of religious perspectives and cultures found in different parts of the world.
Religious Studies exposes students to an immense amount of cultural capital. Students will be introduced to thinkers and ideas that have helped to shape the world around us into what it is today. At HAWI, the aim of the Religious Studies curriculum is to cultivate students that are well-rounded, open-minded and culturally considerate young people. Students will sharpen their critical thinking, analysis and evaluative skills through engaging with different ideas and perspectives.
Literacy is also a central focus in Religious Studies, as students will engage with extracts from a variety of religions and time-periods. Students will be taught to articulate their understanding of the ideas they encounter and clearly explain their personal response to what they have learned. The crafting of one’s opinion takes time and experience, the Religious Studies curriculum at HAWI aims for students to have started building their opinion on various challenging and fundamental questions that are central to adult life and the human experience.
At HAWI, Religious Studies is approached as a highly academic subject. It must be recognised that in modern British society, not everyone would consider themselves religious. To ensure Religious Studies remains highly relevant and useful to students of all belief-systems, the focus on literacy and defending one’s opinion in writing is central to our approach to Religious Studies.
Additionally, we adopt a multi-disciplinary approach at HAWI when teaching Religious Studies. This is based on the simple concept that religious ideas and thinking seep in many different areas of human life. The three broad approaches to religion that students will engage with are: Sociological, Philosophical and Theological. Throughout the KS3 curriculum, students will engage with how religious affects and impacts society and individuals (Sociological approach), the ideas that underpin different religions (Philosophical approach) and the central beliefs and practices of the six main world religions (Theological approach).
